title_en: New Zealand Immigration Reference: The Pros, Cons and Risks
excerpt_en: Is the study-to-residence route to New Zealand still open? A reference, not a verdict — every policy figure checked against official sources, with the teacher shortfall modelled to 2030 and a policy outlook.
body_en:
What is immigration to New Zealand like right now? Does the study → work visa → residence route still work?

This is a reference, not a conclusion. Every policy figure in it has been checked against official sources — Immigration New Zealand, the Teaching Council, NZQA, and the Ministry of Education. The pros, the cons and the risks are all listed; the judgement is yours to make. Policy details are current as of 26 November 2026. Immigration rules change fast — re-check the official websites before you act.

How the route works

The most common route: study for a master's degree in New Zealand, graduate onto a Post Study Work Visa (up to 3 years for a master's), find a job with an accredited employer, stay on a work visa, then get residence through the Skilled Migrant Category (6-point system) or the Green List.

One branch of this is becoming a secondary school teacher. Teaching gets its own section because its barriers and payoffs are both unusual, as explained below.

The teacher shortfall: 2026–2030 (stock-flow model)

The most important question first: how big is the shortfall, and how many years will it last?

The Ministry of Education's Teacher Demand and Supply Projection 2025 (published February 2026) only projects to 2028. The secondary teacher shortfall (medium scenario, the most likely case): about 710 in 2026, 510 in 2027, and 190 in 2028. Primary schools are in surplus over the same period: +530 in 2026, growing to +1,350 by 2028.

There are no official figures for 2029 and 2030. What follows is my own calculation using a stock-flow model — the formula, parameters and data sources are all listed, so it can be checked.

The model:

Supply (next year) = Supply (this year) − Outflows + Inflows
Outflows = Retirements + Moves overseas (including Australia) + Other departures
Inflows = Returning teachers + New domestic graduates + Overseas recruits + Government initiatives

Calibration (2026–2028, Ministry medium scenario):

Demand 30,650 → 30,650 → 30,520; supply 29,940 → 30,140 → 30,330; gap −710 → −510 → −190.

Ministry data: secondary teacher retention 90.5% (2026 projection), so about 9.5% leave each year, roughly 2,860 people; inflows of about 3,050 (net of first-year leavers), so supply grows by roughly 200 a year.

Two key variables on the outflow side for 2029–2030:

1. Retirements. Secondary teachers average 46.0 years old; 30% are aged 55+ (about 9,200 people) and 6.1% are over 65. In the PPTA 2025 survey, retirement accounted for 27% of departures, about 780 a year. As the 55+ cohort moves into ages 60–65, retirements rise by about 25 a year: about 805 in 2029, about 830 in 2030.

2. Moves to Australia. There is no official count of New Zealand teachers moving to Australia. The hard numbers available: in the PPTA survey, 19% of departures were "to go overseas", about 550 a year, with Australia taking the largest share (Victoria alone received several hundred New Zealand teachers in the 12 months to June 2023); in 2025, New Zealand citizens had a net migration loss to Australia of 28,500. The driver is pay: a New South Wales secondary teacher starts on about NZ$104,000, about 69% above New Zealand's starting salary (NZ$61,000). The model assumes about 385 teachers a year move to Australia, rising by about 20 a year: about 405 in 2029, about 425 in 2030.

The general population outflow to Australia is already counted on the demand side: the Ministry's school roll projection uses school-age population figures that include net migration assumptions (about 11,100 in 2025, about 10,200 in 2026, about 12,300 by 2030), which do not offset the fall in births. So demand falls by about 135 teachers a year (rolls fall by about 1,300–1,500 students a year, at a student-teacher ratio of about 1:10.4).

On the inflow side: domestic teacher-education graduates are rising (first-time enrolments up 26% in 2025, completions 785 → 890), adding about 85–120 a year in 2029–2030; overseas recruitment is rising (496 secondary teachers arrived in 2025, up from 446 in all of 2024), adding about 30–40 a year; returning teachers are roughly stable at about 2,310 a year; government initiatives are held at the medium-scenario 800 a year.

Results (figures rounded to the nearest 10):

— 2026: demand 30,650, supply 29,940, gap −710 (official)
— 2027: demand 30,650, supply 30,140, gap −510 (official)
— 2028: demand 30,520, supply 30,330, gap −190 (official)
— 2029: demand about 30,380, supply about 30,620, gap about +240 (model)
— 2030: demand about 30,250, supply about 30,960, gap about +710 (model)

Conclusion: around 2029 the overall secondary teacher shortfall essentially disappears and turns into a small surplus; by 2030 the surplus is about 700. Retirements and moves to Australia together take about 45 extra people a year — they delay the disappearance of the shortfall by only two or three months; they do not change its direction. What closes the gap is demand (school rolls have peaked and are falling) and supply (teacher-education graduates and overseas recruitment are rising) moving at the same time.

What does a small surplus mean? The short answer: it does not mean there are no jobs — but finding one gets harder.

— The surplus is small: +240 is 0.8% of the workforce, +710 is 2.3% — fewer than one to two extra people per 100 secondary teaching jobs. Compared with today's shortfall of 710, supply and demand have flipped, but the jobs have not disappeared.
— About 2,900 vacancies open every year: roughly 9.5% of teachers leave each year through retirement, moves to Australia and career changes, and all of them need replacing. Replacement demand exists even when the headline total is in surplus.
— The shortage subjects stay short: the gaps in maths, science, Māori-medium teaching and rural schools do not disappear with the national total. The Ministry's report states explicitly that shortages in sciences, technology, mathematics and te reo Māori cannot be offset by surpluses in other subjects. In the PPTA survey, one in five vacancies could not be filled, and maths was the hardest to fill.
— For newcomers, competition gets tougher: when schools are not desperate, they pick teachers with local experience and practicum connections first. A newly arrived overseas-trained teacher without New Zealand classroom experience will find the first job harder than today.
— So: jobs are still findable, but it takes the right subject (maths/physics), a willingness to go to hard-to-staff regions and schools, and local connections built during training — and the window is before 2029.

Sensitivity: the model is most sensitive to retention. If retention fell back to 2024's 88.5%, the 2029 gap would still be around −300. If the Australia outflow grew by 50 a year, retirements by 40 a year, and government initiatives fell to the low scenario (675 a year), the 2029 gap would be about +100 and 2030 about +400 — same direction, just a slower surplus. The Ministry's own scenario range is also wide (the 2028 gap runs from −1,480 to +1,180); what matters most is whether initiative funding continues and retention holds.

But a national balance does not mean a job for everyone. Science, Technology and Mathematics, Māori-medium teaching, rural areas and the hardest-to-staff schools will stay short for longer. The Ministry's report states explicitly that shortages in sciences, technology, mathematics and te reo Māori cannot be offset by surpluses in other subjects. A PPTA survey of 155 principals in Term 1 2026: 23% of vacancies had no suitable applicant, 28% had only one, one in five vacancies could not be filled, and maths was among the hardest subjects to fill. Subject shortages outlive the headline shortage.

How remote is "remote", exactly?

First, some scale: New Zealand has only about 5.3 million people, and Auckland (1.55 million) is its largest city. By population, New Zealand has no first- or second-tier cities at all — Auckland is roughly the size of a third-tier Chinese city centre (Yichang about 1.7 million, Luoyang about 2.37 million; third-tier cities include Luoyang, Yichang, Liuzhou and Ganzhou). So "remote" in New Zealand does not mean "far from downtown" — it means "a town of a few thousand people, and the nearest big hospital is hours away by car".

The tier ladder, by urban population:

— Auckland, 1.55 million — a third-tier Chinese city centre (between Yichang's 1.7 million and Luoyang's 2.37 million)
— Christchurch, 408,000 — a fourth-tier city
— Wellington, 210,000 (functional area 441,000) — a fourth-tier city
— Hamilton 192,000, Tauranga 161,000, Dunedin 104,000 — county-level cities
— Invercargill 51,200, Whangārei 56,100, Rotorua 58,500 — county towns
— Gisborne, 38,100 — a county town
— Greymouth 8,610, Kaitaia 6,170, Westport 4,600 — under 10,000 people: townships, one main street
— Chatham Islands 620 people, Stewart Island 380 people — villages

The comparison is by population only — city functions do not scale with population alone. Auckland has an international airport, universities and national headquarters, but its metro, high-speed rail and mall scale are nowhere near a Chinese city of the same population.

Three specific places, item by item — healthcare, transport, shopping:

Greymouth (West Coast, 8,610 people)
— Healthcare: Grey Base Hospital is the only emergency department on the entire West Coast; serious cases go by rescue helicopter to Christchurch. Driving to Christchurch is 241 km, about 3 hours.
— Transport: the nearest airport is Hokitika, with two flights a day to Christchurch (40–45 minutes); Westport had no scheduled flights after 1 May 2026, with service resuming 4 December 2026 at two flights a week (Monday and Friday).
— Shopping: New World and Woolworths, two supermarkets; no Pak'nSave, no mall.

Kaitaia (Far North, 6,170 people)
— Healthcare: a 28-bed hospital serving about 21,000 people; serious cases go to Whangārei (about 150 km, about a 2-hour drive) or by air to Auckland.
— Transport: Barrier Air flies daily to Auckland (50–60 minutes); driving to Auckland takes 4.5–5 hours.
— Shopping: one supermarket in the whole town, a PAK'nSAVE — the first PAK'nSAVE in New Zealand, opened here in 1985.

Gisborne (38,100 people)
— Healthcare: a 110-bed secondary hospital with a 24-hour emergency department.
— Transport: about a 3-hour drive to Napier, about 5 hours to Hamilton (374 km); flights to Auckland take about 1 hour, to Wellington 1–1.5 hours.
— Shopping: PAK'nSAVE and Woolworths; no New World, no large mall.

The extreme cases: the Chatham Islands, 620 people — a doctor-staffed health centre on the island, serious cases airlifted out; a few flights a week, no passenger ferry, one main store. Stewart Island, 380 people — a nurse-led clinic open 10am–12:30pm daily, a GP visiting every second month; a 20-minute flight or a 1-hour ferry to Invercargill; one Four Square supermarket.

What does this have to do with the teacher shortage? The worst regional shortfalls in 2028 are Otago (−6.9%), Auckland South and Southwest (−5.2%), Auckland North and West (−4.8%) and Northland (−2.5%). Note that the West Coast is modelled as a small surplus in 2028 (0 to +10 people) — a regional total says nothing about individual schools, and the Ministry itself warns that individual hard-to-staff schools do not show up in the model. New Zealand has an "isolation index" for schools; schools scoring 1.27 or above get targeted funding, and remote postings come with incentives: an overseas relocation grant of up to NZ$10,000, a teacher bonding scheme of up to NZ$40,000 over five years (185 places a year), and a staffing incentive allowance of NZ$1,000 a year.

The pros

1. Secondary school teachers are on the Green List Tier 1 and can apply for residence directly.

Secondary School Teacher (ANZSCO 241411) is on the Green List Tier 1, eligible for Straight to Residence — no ballot, no queue. Requirements: Teaching Council registration plus a provisional or full practising certificate, an accredited employer, a job of at least 12 months, and pay of at least NZ$35.00 per hour.

2. The Post Study Work Visa window is relatively generous.

A master's graduate who studied full-time in New Zealand for 30+ weeks gets up to 3 years. Compared with countries that send graduates home immediately, that buffer is wide.

3. The Accredited Employer Work Visa no longer has a median wage threshold.

Since 10 March 2025, the AEWV uses market rate plus the minimum wage instead. Requirements: an accredited employer plus an approved job check, at least 30 hours a week, two years of relevant work experience or a Level 4+ qualification (a bachelor's in any field counts).

4. The 2026 reforms did not close every door.

On 24 August 2026 the Skilled Migrant Category was overhauled into three pathways, with extra points for New Zealand qualifications and faster work-experience points. From 23 November 2026 the Post Study Work Visa was widened, with a new six-month Short-Term Graduate Work Visa, and a Level 7 Graduate Diploma plus a bachelor's now qualifies for a Post Study Work Visa (up to one year).

The cons

1. The language bar is hard: IELTS 7.0 in every skill.

The Teaching Council's current policy (effective 21 January 2026): IELTS Academic 7.0 in every skill and overall, valid within two years, with One Skill Retake accepted. Alternatives exist — PTE, Cambridge, TOEFL and others have equivalent scores. 7.0 in every skill is still a hard bar for most people.

2. An overseas degree does not qualify you to register as a teacher — you must complete a teacher education programme first.

NZQA's Teaching International Qualification Assessment only recognises qualifications "developed specifically to prepare a learner to become a teacher". An ordinary overseas bachelor's degree is not one of them. To teach, you must first complete a Graduate Diploma of Teaching (Secondary, one year) or a Master of Teaching and Learning (Secondary, eleven months) in New Zealand. That is a year of tuition, living costs and time.

3. Teaching subjects need to reach 300-level, and whether yours count is assessed case by case.

Entry to the Graduate Diploma (Secondary) requires a bachelor's degree with teaching subjects studied to 300-level (third-year level), ideally a second subject to 200-level, plus an interview, literacy and numeracy checks, and police vetting. The Master of Teaching and Learning at Victoria University of Wellington requires a GPA of 5.0 (B average), has only 30 places a year, and requires an in-person selection day in Wellington. Whether the maths and physics content of an undergraduate degree counts as teaching subjects has no general answer — it is assessed transcript by transcript.

4. Finding a job is the biggest hurdle.

If you cannot find an accredited employer, your work visa expires and you go home. The posts are genuinely short of people, but the bar screens most people out. What is short is "people who meet all the conditions" — not "people who want to teach".

5. The Green List is not open on graduation day.

Immigration New Zealand itself warns that teaching roles may not meet the pay requirement — new graduates are unlikely to qualify immediately. In the Skilled Migrant Category, the 5 points for teacher registration require "registration and a Full 1 or Full 2 practising certificate"; a new graduate holds a provisional certificate, which does not count. You need to work for some years and upgrade to a Full certificate before these points apply.

6. Classroom management is a second bar.

Passing the language test is only the ticket in; classroom management and communicating with local students are a different skill set.

The risks

1. The policy itself is moving, and moving fast.

The ACT Party proposal is the example: ACT proposed on 1 September 2026 to abolish the Permanent Resident Visa, change resident visa travel conditions to five years, and require 730 days of residence in any rolling five years. But on 26 October 2026 ACT dropped the abolition of the PRV in its manifesto, keeping only a two-in-five-years presence requirement. This is party policy only — not coalition policy, and not law. Preliminary results of the 7 November 2026 election: National 42, ACT 13, NZ First 12 — 67 of 131 seats; the official result is due on 27 November 2026. The policy direction will only be clear after the official result.

2. The big trend is "more selective", not "closed".

Over the next 10–20 years, the key word for immigration policy is not "fewer" but "more selective". OECD International Migration Outlook 2025 (3 November 2025): OECD countries received about 6.2 million permanent migrants in 2024, about 15% above 2019, but down 4% from the post-pandemic peak. World Bank Global Economic Prospects (June 2025): if forecasts materialise, average global growth in the first seven years of the 2020s will be the slowest of any decade since the 1960s — note the conditional wording, not an established fact.

Low growth, AI replacing some jobs, and the return of national-security logic — combined, the entry for ordinary low-skilled jobs will narrow further, and the immigration value of standardised white-collar jobs may fall. Doctors, nurses, engineers, senior technicians with genuinely scarce skills, and AI talent will be worth more and more. The state is starting to pick migrants the way it picks assets.

3. The stability of resident status is no longer a given.

From 1990 to around 2015, the practical gap between citizens, permanent residents and long-term residents in everyday life kept shrinking, and citizenship came to feel like "a passport plus the vote". But if the world increasingly emphasises geopolitical competition, industrial policy, technology controls, financial sanctions and critical-infrastructure security, the rights gap between citizens and residents is likely to widen again.

There are historical precedents: during both world wars, the UK, Australia, New Zealand and Canada all ran registration, travel restrictions and internment for so-called "enemy aliens"; in 1942 Canada forcibly relocated more than 20,000 residents of Japanese descent, and the Canadian government today admits there was insufficient evidence they posed a real security threat. That does not mean history will repeat itself — it means the stability of a foreign resident's rights depends heavily on the international order as a whole. Getting PR no longer carries the same "basically permanent and stable" assumption it did in 1995 or 2005.

4. The investment is large and the timeline is long — do not bet everything on it.

Think in years: one year of teacher education, then finding a job, then working up to a Full certificate. It is not graduation straight to residence. Tuition, living costs and time all have to be counted. Whichever way you choose, it is very hard — be careful, follow the rules, and do not bet everything on one throw.

Policy outlook

The following is my own forecast based on the information available — not official news:

— The official election result is due on 27 November 2026. Once a coalition is formed, ACT's "two years in five" presence requirement may enter the legislative process; the abolition of the PRV has already been dropped, so there is no short-term need to worry about PR itself being abolished, but resident visa travel conditions and residence requirements may tighten.
— The Green List changes take effect on 8 March 2027, with secondary school teachers unaffected; the next Green List review (most likely within 2027) may keep narrowing Tier 2, while teachers' Tier 1 status will most likely hold in the short term — because the shortfall is still there.
— The Skilled Migrant Category 6-point system was overhauled in August 2026, so another major change in the short term is unlikely; but the pay threshold (NZ$35.00 per hour) is adjusted annually with the median wage and will most likely rise in 2027.
— The Post Study Work Visa widening took effect on 23 November 2026 — a window for now.
— The model shows the overall secondary teacher shortfall essentially disappearing around 2029, so the policy tailwind for the teaching route may fade around then — not that the route closes after 2029, but that "we are short of people", its strongest policy argument, gets weaker.

Key figures at a glance

— Teacher registration language: IELTS Academic 7.0 in every skill and overall (policy from 21 January 2026)
— Post Study Work Visa: master's studied 30+ weeks, up to 3 years
— Skilled Migrant Category: New Zealand master's 6 points; overseas master's plus bachelor's 5 points; doctorate 6 points
— Skilled employment pay: at least NZ$35.00 per hour (ANZSCO skill levels 1–3); median wage NZ$35.00 per hour (from 9 March 2026)
— Teacher registration points: 5 points, requires Full 1/Full 2 practising certificate; provisional does not count
— Secondary teacher shortfall: about 710 in 2026, 510 in 2027, 190 in 2028 (official); about +240 in 2029, about +710 in 2030 (stock-flow model — a small surplus)
— OECD permanent migration 2024: about 6.2 million, 15% above 2019, down 4% from the post-pandemic peak

Recent policy changes (2026)

— 24 August 2026: Skilled Migrant Category overhaul — three pathways, extra points for New Zealand qualifications, faster work-experience points.
— From 23 November 2026: Post Study Work Visa widened, plus a new six-month Short-Term Graduate Work Visa; Level 7 Graduate Diploma plus a bachelor's now qualifies for a Post Study Work Visa (up to one year).
— Announced 3 November 2026, effective 8 March 2027: Green List changes — 17 Tier 2 roles removed, four special education teachers move from Tier 2 to Tier 1; secondary school teachers unaffected.
